The broader problem has a clear place in economic theory. Douglass North asked why an increase in a region’s export income sometimes supported a more varied economy and sometimes left it dependent on a narrow range of production. His 1959 treatment emphasized both the character of the export activity and the disposition of the income it brought in.[^29]

An export here means a sale outside the region, including elsewhere in the United States. Cuervo’s livestock and wool connections are examples of such trade. They brought the surrounding producers into markets larger than local consumption could have sustained. That connection was a source of opportunity, even when later stages of production took place elsewhere.

North’s argument directs attention to what the export requires locally. An activity may need substantial handling, storage, repair and other supporting work. It may also rely on services most efficiently supplied elsewhere. Some of its income reaches local workers and firms; some pays distant suppliers or accrues to owners who spend it in other places. The resulting town depends on this distribution of work and expenditure.

Cuervo’s early record identifies several local contributions. Bond & Wiest supplied merchandise and credit, handled products, maintained livestock interests and arranged market relationships. The warehouse and freight arrangements gave some of those transactions a reason to gather there. These were real commercial functions, with reported profits over a substantial interval.

The record also places limits on the growth expected from them. Sheep sent to Kansas for feeding supported a stage of production outside Cuervo. Wool buyers in Boston belonged to a market extending beyond the village. Feed manufactured in Clovis could be sold by a Cuervo dealer. The town participated in these chains without containing every activity in them.

This is why a productive ranching district need not produce a large town at each shipping point. The location of production is only part of the location of employment. A place might assemble substantial quantities of a commodity while retaining a modest amount of handling and commercial work. Another center might combine distribution, finance, administration and processing. The two can grow differently while serving the same broad economy.

The question is consequently more demanding than whether higher livestock prices should have produced shops. Shops and other services did exist at Cuervo. The issue is why that range of provision remained limited, how individual activities were sustained and what later allowed some of them to be supplied elsewhere. Those outcomes depend on the organization of demand as well as its total value.

## Different requirements for staying open

The merchant’s wide market and the garage’s combined tasks helped make local business possible. The school, doctor proposal and newspaper reveal additional requirements: an essential worker, dependable receipts and a backer’s willingness to pay. Their sponsors also cared about what was offered. Hicks wanted a first-class weekly; school supporters wanted practical instruction and considered high-school accreditation. A count of potential users could not resolve those decisions.

These commitments could change at different times. A political purpose might be fulfilled while pupils still needed instruction; a new mechanic could reopen a garage while another enterprise lost support. Their uneven histories help explain why no single population count marks the point at which Cuervo’s services became untenable.

The next chapter follows the people within that changing provision. Schooling, work and residence could connect a household to different places, with each connection changing on its own schedule.

Those connections helped determine what the settlement provided and what it obtained from outside.

A population total fixes people within a reporting boundary at one date. Ages, households, occupations and dated family histories reveal more of the arrangements behind it. Cuervo changed in composition as well as size.

The schedules show a larger change in how they lived: household groups increased from forty-two to fifty-nine, with most of the additional groups containing only one or two people. The counts covered countryside as well as the village. Following the people within them reveals arrivals, changing families, and several kinds of work under one roof. Later family histories trace a different set of connections: where people went to school, earned a living, and made a home.

Los Lunas supplies the latter contrast. Its household population rose from 5,936 in 1990 to 16,994 in 2020, an increase of about 186 percent. Santa Rosa’s household population rose by less than one percent over the same period. Separating group quarters leaves the contrast intact.[^22]

A fixed study rectangle around the settlement illustrates the difficulty. It covers about 6.28 square kilometers, including some surrounding land. before: These findings connect the institutions of the previous chapter with the transport history that follows. A place could lose a service while residents found another way to reach it. Distance therefore needs to be translated into the actual demands of a trip. A passenger had to reach the departure point, wait for the service and arrange the return. A controlled-access highway changes the relationship between a traveler and roadside premises. On an ordinary road, a driver may pass a shopfront and turn directly into its entrance. A business located beside the old road may remain reachable while receiving fewer unplanned visits. The physical presence of an interchange is therefore insufficient evidence that commercial access remained equivalent.

The family histories give this wider geography a residential dimension. Education, employment, property and family ties could connect the same person to several places.

The broader consequence is that a locality can become less self-contained without immediately becoming empty. Households may obtain more of what they need elsewhere while remaining near their land or home. Other households may move but keep property, relatives or institutional connections. The modern census provides bounds for selected study areas rather than a secure count for the built village. Blocks extend beyond the buildings and change between enumerations, limiting what their populations can establish about the locality.[^11]

The railway gave an established merchant a reason to move from Cabra. Capital, premises, management and customer relationships made that location usable; schooling and other services gave additional reasons to gather. Santa Rosa already performed a wider range of work, but Cuervo did not need to reproduce it to serve a useful market.

The more demanding question is how much of the surrounding economy a place could continue to serve. Ranching required land and access to markets. It did not require every purchase, loan, shipment or household service to occur in the same village. Cuervo’s businesses had to retain a useful part in those activities.
